---
title: "Sound 10: Granular Synthesis"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

Take a few seconds of recorded sound and cut it into hundreds of tiny pieces, each a few
hundredths of a second long, each faded in and out so it doesn't click. These are **grains**. Play them
back overlapping, dozens a second, and you can do things a tape never could: hold one moment of a sound
forever, stretch a sound to ten times its length without making it lower, or scatter it into a
glittering cloud. That's **granular synthesis**. The idea goes back to the composer Iannis Xenakis in
the 1950s, who cut tape into tiny pieces with scissors.

**How to use the page.** Pick a **sound to cut up** (or record three seconds of your own voice), press
▶, and move the **Position**. The strip shows the sound; each flash is one grain being read.

## The grain cloud

<div class="sk" data-w="granular"></div>

- **Position**: where in the sound the grains are read from.
- **Scan speed**: how fast the position moves on its own. At ×1 it plays the sound at normal speed; at
  ×0.2 it plays it five times slower, but **at the same pitch**, because each grain still plays at the
  normal speed. At 0 the sound is **frozen**.
- **Grain size**: under about 20 ms each grain is a click, and you hear the *rate* of the clicks as a
  buzz. From 50 to 200 ms you hear the sound itself, smeared.
- **Grains per second**: few grains give a crackle; many give a smooth cloud.
- **Spray**: each grain is read from a slightly random place near the position. More spray, more blur.
- **Pitch** and **Random pitch**: each grain can be played faster or slower. With random pitch the
  grains turn into a shimmering chord.
- **Backwards grains** and **Stereo spread** make the cloud stranger and wider.

## Try this

1. **Freeze** on *Vowels*. Move the position slowly through the sound: you can stop on any vowel and
   hold it.
2. **Stretch (slow motion)** on the *Synth riff*: the riff, five times slower, at its normal pitch.
   Video editors and DJs use this to fit a sound to a length without changing the key.
3. **Shimmer**: the grains an octave up and spread wide. Ambient music lives here.
4. Record your own voice and choose **Scatter**.
5. Play the keys: the whole cloud moves to the note you play, a melody made from your voice.

## Where you've heard it

Time-stretching in every DAW (Ableton's warp modes, Melodyne) is granular underneath. So are the
"frozen" pads of ambient music, the shimmering textures of film scores, and many synths: Ableton's
Granulator, Mutable Instruments' Clouds, the Tasty Chips GR-1. The [glitch](sound-delay.qmd) effects
and the freeze button on the [reverb page](sound-reverb.qmd) use grains too.
